2. The disputed land compromising a tank on plot No. 131 and recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 1 belonged to petitioner and others in Taluki Right appertaining Touzi No. 358. The tank in question was taken away by the Comilla Municipality for management. The opposite party No. 1 took lease of the tank under the Comilla Municipality for a term of 12 years commencing from January, 1955 "and executed an agreement on 3-2-55. The opposite party No. 1 was in possession of the tank as a lessee under the Municipality and filed Title Suit No. 109 of 1967 for partition of the said tank. The petitioner and other co-sharers were impleaded in the said partition suit. The petitioner on receipt of summons along with a copy of the plaint came to know that one Taiyabun nessa, wife of O.P. No. 1 took a kabala dated 10-8-55 from Atul Chandra Das who took settlement of the land from one Shabmhu Charan by a kabuliya dated 5-9-46. Shambhu Charan took lease under the Talukdars Bardhans in the berami of Debendra Nath Chattarjee in the year 1943 or 1944. The petitioner thus came to know of the transfer made by Atul Chandra Das in favour of Taiyabunnessa on 8-41-67. The petitioner contends that he had no prior knowledge of the transfer. No notice of the said transfer was served upon him. Since the tank was in possession of the O.P. No. 1 as a lessee of the Municipality, he had no occasion to know about the alleged transfer. According to the petitioner, Taiyabunnessa was a stranger to the land. Taiyabunnessa died leaving O.P. Nos. 1 to 7 as heirs. On these allegations the application for pre-emption has been filed upon necessary statutory deposit. 

 6. Mr. Salam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner contends that the petitioner is a co-sharer in the land. According to him after the acquisition of superior interest, the petitioner become a tenant in respect of the disputed lard along with other tenants including Atul Chandra Das. The learned Advocate submits that the property in suit being a tank is impartible in nature and as such the pre-emptor become a co-sharer in joint ownership and possession with ether tenants. Mr. Salary has Prefaced his contention by referring to the decision in the case of, Anwara Begunm Chowdhurani and Shamsul Huda Chowdhury Vs. Nur Jahan Begum and others reported in 27 DLR (Appellate Division) 109. There is no dispute with the proposition that after the notification issued under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the status of an under raiyat was upgraded to that of a tenant. There is also no dispute that with the acquisition of rent-receiving interests by the Government, all the intermediary interests disappeared and a person holding land under the landlord became a tenant holding land directly under the Government. These aspects of law have no direct reference to the question raised by the learned Advocate. The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act did not contemplate the merger of all the existing tenancies into one common tenancy and all the tenants under the different tenancies become co-sharers in such a tenancy. The facts of the instant case clearly indicate that the petitioner was a co-sharer of the Touzi No. 358 recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 1. There is no dispute that Hemanga Mohan Bardhan was a co-sharer in the said Khatian. No. 1. This Bardhan settled some land of the disputed tank in favour of Shambhu Charan Misir. The settlement obtained by Shambhu Charan constituted a tenancy distinct and separate from the holding recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 1. It further appears that Shambhu Charan settled the suit land in favour of Atul Chandra Das by a registered Kabuliyat Exhibit B dated 5. 9. 46 in raiyati right. Thus the raiyati right of Atul Chandra Das constituted a holding which was different from the holding of Shambhu Charan and the holding recorded C. S. Khatian No. 1. On an analysis of these facts, it transpires that the contention of Mr. Salain, leads to an absurd proposition of law. By no stretch of imagination it can be conceived that with the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act coming into force, all these three holdings merged into one holding and all the tenants in respect of these different holdings became co-sharers to one common holding, in other words a co-tenancy emerged. The effect of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is that the intermediary interests ceased to exist and the tenants who were holding as under-tenants became tenants directly under the Government. Mr. Salam, however, could not cite any authority in support of his proposition. He has, however, referred to the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury and another Vs. Musammat Rezia Begum and another 16 DLR 77 to contend that Atul Chandra Das, Shambhu Charan and Bardhan became co-sharers with the petitioner. The principle laid down in the said case does not extend any Support to the view Mr. Salim has advanced. He has relied upon the following passage from the case of Brindaban Chandra: 

 7. Further, on the date of the transfer namely, 10-8-55 the petitioner was not a co-sharer in a tenancy in respect of the land. Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act cud not come in operation to invest a person with a right which was not available to him on the date of transfer. Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act makes no reference to any retrospective operation of the right of pre-emption. Thus, in any view of the matter whether the properly is partible or not, whether or not the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act made the petitioner a tenant in respect of the land held by him under khatian No. 1, the petitioner was not a co-sharer having a right of pre-emption under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.
